summary: Metabolic bone disease covers conditions where bone building or bone breakdown goes wrong at the cell or hormone level. This unit centers on osteopetrosis (osteoclasts cannot resorb bone) and renal osteodystrophy, and teaches the lab pattern for each major bone disease. Exams love the calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and PTH table.

points: Osteoclasts fail to resorb bone, so old bone is never removed and remodeled.
Osteoclasts need an acid pump and a chloride channel to dissolve mineral; loss of either stops resorption.
Causes: carbonic anhydrase II deficiency (no H+ supply), CLCN7 chloride channel mutations, TCIRG1 proton pump subunit mutations.
Carbonic anhydrase II deficiency also causes renal tubular acidosis and cerebral calcification.
Result: thick, dense, marble-like bone that is brittle and fractures easily.
notes.why: An osteoclast seals onto bone and pumps protons into the sealed resorption pit through a vacuolar H+-ATPase (TCIRG1 encodes a subunit), while the ClC-7 chloride channel lets chloride follow, making hydrochloric acid that dissolves hydroxyapatite. Carbonic anhydrase II supplies those protons by forming carbonic acid from CO2 and water. Breaking any link stops resorption, so bone piles up without remodeling into organized lamellae, which makes it dense but brittle. Carbonic anhydrase II also works in renal tubule cells, which explains the renal tubular acidosis.

points: Infantile autosomal recessive form: severe, presents in infancy, often fatal in childhood without treatment.
Adult autosomal dominant form (Albers-Schonberg disease): milder, often found by fractures or on x-ray.
Bone fills the marrow space, causing anemia, thrombocytopenia, and infections (pancytopenia).
Extramedullary hematopoiesis enlarges the liver and spleen.
Narrowed skull foramina compress cranial nerves II, VII, and VIII: vision loss, facial palsy, hearing loss.
Osteomyelitis of the jaw is common because dense bone has poor blood supply.
X-ray: diffusely dense bones, bone-in-bone, Erlenmeyer flask flaring of the distal femur.
Osteoclasts come from the monocyte-macrophage line, so stem cell transplant can cure the infantile form.
notes.why: Osteoclasts hollow out the marrow cavity during growth, so when they fail the space for blood cell production never opens and hematopoiesis moves to the liver and spleen. Skull foramina also enlarge by resorption as the child grows, so they stay narrow and squeeze the optic, facial, and vestibulocochlear nerves. Osteoclasts arise from hematopoietic stem cells of the monocyte-macrophage lineage, so donor stem cells can supply working osteoclasts, which is why transplant cures the infantile form.

points: Osteoporosis: calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and PTH all normal.
Paget disease: only alkaline phosphatase is high.
Osteomalacia and rickets (vitamin D deficiency): low calcium and phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase and PTH.
Primary hyperparathyroidism: high calcium and PTH, low phosphate.
Renal osteodystrophy: low calcium, high phosphate, high PTH, high alkaline phosphatase.
Alkaline phosphatase rises when osteoblasts are busy; it stays normal when bone is only lost.
notes.why: Each pattern follows from what controls calcium and phosphate. PTH raises serum calcium and makes the kidney waste phosphate, so primary PTH excess gives high calcium with low phosphate, while a secondary PTH rise is a response to low calcium. Vitamin D deficiency cuts gut absorption of both minerals, and the resulting low calcium drives PTH up. Alkaline phosphatase comes from active osteoblasts, so it climbs when bone formation is busy (Paget disease, osteomalacia, renal bone disease) and stays normal in osteoporosis, where bone is lost quietly.

points: Chronic kidney disease cannot excrete phosphate, so phosphate rises and binds calcium.
Damaged kidneys make less 1-alpha-hydroxylase, so calcitriol falls and gut calcium absorption drops; high FGF23 lowers calcitriol further.
Low calcium, high phosphate, and low calcitriol drive parathyroid hyperplasia (secondary hyperparathyroidism).
High PTH causes osteitis fibrosa cystica: subperiosteal resorption (radial side of the middle phalanges), salt and pepper skull, bone cysts.
Brown tumors are masses of osteoclast-like giant cells, fibrous tissue, and hemorrhage; hemosiderin makes them brown.
Low calcitriol also causes defective mineralization (osteomalacia), and chronic acidosis leaches bone buffer.
Long-standing secondary disease can become autonomous (tertiary hyperparathyroidism) with high calcium.
notes.why: Falling GFR retains phosphate, which raises FGF23 from osteocytes; FGF23 suppresses renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase, and loss of renal mass removes more of the enzyme, so calcitriol falls early. Low calcitriol reduces gut calcium absorption and releases the parathyroid from vitamin D receptor restraint, while high phosphate and low calcium directly stimulate PTH secretion and gland growth. Sustained PTH drives osteoclastic resorption. Over years the hyperplastic glands lose calcium-sensing and vitamin D receptors, so they keep secreting PTH even when calcium is high (tertiary disease).

charts.title: Osteopetrosis forms
rows: TCIRG1, CLCN7; carbonic anhydrase II in a milder recessive variant with renal tubular acidosis
Often fatal in childhood without stem cell transplant
Fractures, osteoarthritis, jaw osteomyelitis; normal lifespan

tricks.label: Marble bone
tricks.text: Marble is hard, heavy, and shatters. Osteopetrosis bone is dense, fills the marrow cavity, and breaks easily.

tricks.label: Who uses the ALP?
tricks.text: Alkaline phosphatase tracks osteoblast work. Bone that is only being lost (osteoporosis) has normal ALP; bone being rebuilt or poorly mineralized (Paget, osteomalacia, hyperparathyroid bone) has high ALP.

tricks.label: Kidney failure chain
tricks.text: Phosphate up, calcitriol down, calcium down, PTH up, bone eaten. Trace these five steps in order and the lab pattern writes itself.

highYield: Osteopetrosis is a failure of osteoclast resorption, giving dense but brittle bone.
Carbonic anhydrase II deficiency combines osteopetrosis with renal tubular acidosis.
Marrow obliteration in osteopetrosis causes pancytopenia with hepatosplenomegaly from extramedullary hematopoiesis.
Narrow foramina in osteopetrosis cause blindness and deafness.
Osteoporosis has all-normal bone labs; Paget disease has an isolated high alkaline phosphatase.
Renal osteodystrophy shows high phosphate, low calcium, and high PTH.
Brown tumors and subperiosteal resorption of the phalanges mark osteitis fibrosa cystica from high PTH.
pitfalls: Osteopetrosis and osteoporosis sound alike but are opposites: too much bone versus too little bone.
Primary hyperparathyroidism has low phosphate; secondary hyperparathyroidism from kidney failure has high phosphate.
Dense bone on x-ray does not mean strong bone; osteopetrotic bone fractures easily.
A brown tumor is a reactive lesion of hyperparathyroidism and is easy to mistake for a true giant cell tumor of bone.

flows.title: Renal osteodystrophy
steps: Falling GFR retains phosphate and raises FGF23 from osteocytes.
FGF23 and lost renal mass reduce 1-alpha-hydroxylase, so calcitriol falls.
Low calcitriol cuts gut calcium absorption, and serum calcium falls.
Low calcium, high phosphate, and low calcitriol drive parathyroid hyperplasia.
High PTH drives osteoclastic resorption: osteitis fibrosa cystica.
Years later, autonomous glands can cause tertiary hyperparathyroidism with high calcium.

flows.title: Osteoclast bone resorption (fails in osteopetrosis)
steps: Osteoclast seals onto the bone surface, enclosing a resorption pit.
Carbonic anhydrase II forms carbonic acid from CO2 and water.
Carbonic acid splits into H+ and bicarbonate; bicarbonate exits in exchange for chloride.
Vacuolar H+-ATPase pumps H+ into the pit; ClC-7 lets chloride follow.
Hydrochloric acid dissolves hydroxyapatite; cathepsin K digests exposed collagen.

summary: Congenital musculoskeletal diseases come from single-gene defects in structural proteins: fibrillin (Marfan), dystrophin (muscular dystrophy), collagen (osteogenesis imperfecta, Ehlers-Danlos), and a growth plate receptor (achondroplasia). Exams link each gene to its protein, its inheritance, and its classic physical findings.

points: Autosomal dominant FBN1 mutation on chromosome 15; fibrillin-1 forms microfibrils that scaffold elastic fibers.
Fibrillin normally holds latent TGF-beta; defective fibrillin releases it, so excess TGF-beta signaling weakens tissue.
Tall and thin, long limbs, arm span greater than height, arachnodactyly, pectus excavatum or carinatum, joint hypermobility, scoliosis.
Lens dislocates upward (superotemporal ectopia lentis).
Aortic root dilation from medial degeneration (cystic medial necrosis) leads to aortic regurgitation and dissection, the main cause of death.
Mitral valve prolapse and spontaneous pneumothorax are also common.
notes.why: Fibrillin-1 microfibrils are the scaffold on which elastin is laid down, and they also anchor latent TGF-beta in the matrix. Mutant fibrillin weakens the scaffold and lets TGF-beta escape, and excess signaling degrades the aortic media. The tissues hit hardest are those that depend on microfibrils: the aortic root, which bears the greatest pulsatile stress; the ciliary zonules, which are made of fibrillin and hold the lens; and ligaments and joint capsules, which become lax.

points: Homocystinuria: autosomal recessive, usually cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency, with high homocysteine.
Shares a tall, Marfan-like body build.
Lens dislocates downward (inferonasal); intellectual disability and arterial and venous thrombosis are present.
Marfan has normal intelligence and no clotting tendency.
notes.why: Cystathionine beta-synthase uses vitamin B6 to join homocysteine and serine into cystathionine, the first step toward cysteine. When it fails, homocysteine accumulates, injures endothelium, and promotes thrombosis in arteries and veins. Homocysteine is also thought to disrupt fibrillin by interfering with its disulfide bonds, which would explain the Marfan-like build and lens dislocation. Thrombosis and intellectual disability have no counterpart in Marfan syndrome, so they separate the two quickly.

points: X-linked recessive DMD gene; dystrophin links the actin cytoskeleton to the dystroglycan complex and extracellular matrix.
Duchenne: frameshift deletions or nonsense mutations give absent dystrophin, so the membrane tears with each contraction and fibers die.
Boys under 5: proximal weakness, waddling gait, Gowers sign (uses hands to climb up the legs to stand).
Calf pseudohypertrophy: muscle replaced by fat and fibrous tissue.
CK very high (often 10 to 100 times normal) from birth.
Death in early adulthood from dilated cardiomyopathy or respiratory failure; scoliosis worsens breathing.
Becker: in-frame deletions give a shorter, partly working dystrophin; onset later, slower course, walking into adulthood.
Immunostaining: dystrophin absent in Duchenne, reduced or patchy in Becker; genetic deletion and duplication testing confirms the type.
notes.why: Dystrophin tethers actin under the sarcolemma to the dystroglycan complex, which binds laminin in the basement membrane, so contractile force passes to the matrix without stressing the membrane. Without it, each contraction tears the sarcolemma, CK leaks out, calcium floods in, proteases activate, and the fiber dies; repeated cycles exhaust satellite cell repair. The reading frame rule predicts severity: frameshift or nonsense mutations make no functional protein (Duchenne), while in-frame deletions keep both ends of the protein and make a shorter, partly working dystrophin (Becker).

points: Mostly autosomal dominant COL1A1 or COL1A2 mutations: defective or too little type I collagen.
Glycine substitutions break the Gly-X-Y triple helix and act as dominant negatives; type I (mildest) makes too little normal collagen; type II is lethal around birth.
Multiple fractures with minimal trauma, bowed bones, short stature, wormian bones.
Blue sclerae (thin collagen lets the choroid show), conductive hearing loss (abnormal ossicles), dentinogenesis imperfecta (opalescent, fragile teeth), joint laxity.
notes.why: Type I collagen is two alpha-1 chains (COL1A1) and one alpha-2 chain (COL1A2) wound into a triple helix in which every third residue must be glycine, the only amino acid small enough to fit the helix core. A glycine substitution kinks the helix, and because mutant chains join trimers with normal chains, one bad allele ruins most molecules (dominant negative effect), giving severe forms. A null allele only halves normal collagen output, giving mild type I. Every type I collagen tissue shows the defect: bone, sclera, dentin, ossicles, and ligaments.

points: Favors abuse: posterior rib fractures, metaphyseal corner fractures, fractures of different ages, bruises in a non-mobile infant, retinal hemorrhage, a story that does not fit.
Favors osteogenesis imperfecta: blue sclerae, dentinogenesis imperfecta, wormian bones, low bone density, bowing, family history of fractures or hearing loss.
notes.why: Abuse fractures come from forces an infant cannot produce alone. Squeezing the chest levers the posterior ribs against the transverse processes, and shaking or yanking a limb shears the weak metaphysis, giving corner fractures. Fractures at different stages of healing show repeated events. Osteogenesis imperfecta instead leaves signs in other type I collagen tissues and in bone quality itself, such as blue sclerae, abnormal dentin, wormian bones, and diffuse osteopenia, so those features point toward a collagen disorder.

points: Ehlers-Danlos: a group of collagen disorders with stretchy skin, hypermobile and dislocating joints, easy bruising, poor wound healing.
Classic type: type V collagen (COL5A1, COL5A2). Vascular type: type III collagen (COL3A1), with arterial, bowel, and uterine rupture.
Achondroplasia: autosomal dominant FGFR3 gain of function that slows growth plate chondrocytes (endochondral bone).
Rhizomelic shortening (upper arms and thighs) with normal trunk length, macrocephaly, frontal bossing, normal intelligence.
Most cases are new mutations linked to older paternal age.
notes.why: In Ehlers-Danlos syndrome the affected tissue follows where the defective collagen matters most: type V collagen regulates type I fibril assembly in skin and joints, while type III collagen is abundant in vessel walls, bowel, and uterus, so the vascular type ruptures those organs. Achondroplasia is a gain of function in FGFR3, a receptor that normally brakes chondrocyte proliferation in the growth plate. Constant signaling slows endochondral growth, so long bones are short, while intramembranous bone such as the skull vault grows normally and looks large.

COL1A1 or COL1A2, type I collagen

Classic: COL5A1 or COL5A2 (type V). Vascular: COL3A1 (type III)
Faulty collagen in skin, joints, and vessels

tricks.label: Patients can't BITE
tricks.text: Osteogenesis imperfecta: Bones (multiple fractures), I (eye: blue sclerae), Teeth (dentinogenesis imperfecta), Ear (hearing loss).

tricks.label: Marfan looks up, homocystinuria looks down
tricks.text: Marfan lens goes up and out; homocystinuria lens goes down and in. The patient with clots and intellectual disability is the one looking down.

tricks.label: Reading frame rule
tricks.text: Frameshift deletion scrambles every codon after it, so no dystrophin (Duchenne). In-frame deletion skips a chunk but keeps reading, so a short dystrophin (Becker).

highYield: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant FBN1 (fibrillin-1) defect with excess TGF-beta signaling.
Aortic root dilation and dissection are the main threats to life in Marfan syndrome.
Upward lens dislocation suggests Marfan; downward lens dislocation suggests homocystinuria.
Duchenne: absent dystrophin, Gowers sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, very high CK, death from cardiomyopathy or respiratory failure.
Becker: truncated dystrophin from an in-frame deletion, later onset, milder course.
Osteogenesis imperfecta is a type I collagen defect with fractures, blue sclerae, hearing loss, and dentinogenesis imperfecta.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos (type III collagen) causes arterial and bowel rupture.
Achondroplasia is an FGFR3 gain of function with rhizomelic shortening and normal intelligence.
pitfalls: Calf pseudohypertrophy is fat and fibrous tissue, so big calves do not mean strong muscle.
Becker is not just mild Duchenne in time; check dystrophin staining (reduced versus absent) and the type of deletion.
Multiple fractures in a child are not automatically abuse; look for blue sclerae, abnormal teeth, and family history before deciding.
Osteogenesis imperfecta is type I collagen (bone); classic Ehlers-Danlos is type V and vascular Ehlers-Danlos is type III.
A Marfan-like build with thrombosis and learning problems points to homocystinuria.

flows.title: Duchenne muscular dystrophy
steps: Frameshift or nonsense DMD mutation leaves muscle with no dystrophin.
Actin is no longer anchored to the dystroglycan complex and matrix.
Contraction tears the sarcolemma; CK leaks out and calcium floods in.
Calcium activates proteases, and muscle fibers undergo necrosis.
Repeated cycles exhaust regeneration; fat and fibrous tissue replace muscle.
Progressive weakness ends in respiratory failure or dilated cardiomyopathy.

flows.title: Marfan aortic disease
steps: FBN1 mutation produces defective fibrillin-1 microfibrils.
Elastic fibers lose their scaffold, and latent TGF-beta is released.
Excess TGF-beta signaling degrades the aortic media (cystic medial degeneration).
The aortic root dilates under pulsatile stress.
Annular dilation causes aortic regurgitation; an intimal tear causes dissection.

flows.title: Osteogenesis imperfecta from a glycine substitution
steps: Missense mutation replaces a glycine in a COL1A1 or COL1A2 Gly-X-Y repeat.
Mutant chains join normal chains and kink the triple helix (dominant negative).
Abnormal procollagen is degraded or forms faulty fibrils.
Bone matrix is scant and weak, so bones fracture with minimal trauma.

summary: Degenerative musculoskeletal diseases come from wear, aging, hormone loss, or lost blood supply: osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, Paget disease, and avascular necrosis. This unit also covers pediatric hip and knee disorders, disc herniation, and Dupuytren contracture. Exams test the mechanism, the typical patient, and the findings that separate look-alikes.

points: Chondrocyte injury and mechanical stress cause loss of proteoglycan and type II collagen.
Cartilage fibrillates and cracks; exposed bone polishes smooth (eburnation).
Subchondral sclerosis and cysts form; osteophytes grow at the joint margins.
Risk: age, obesity, prior joint injury, heavy mechanical load, joint malalignment.
Pain worse with use and better with rest; morning stiffness under 30 minutes.
Asymmetric weight-bearing joints (knees, hips, spine), first CMC, Heberden (DIP) and Bouchard (PIP) nodes; MCPs and wrists usually spared.
X-ray: joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts; synovial fluid noninflammatory.
notes.why: Cartilage resists load because aggrecan holds water under pressure inside a type II collagen network. Mechanical stress and aging push chondrocytes into a catabolic state in which IL-1, matrix metalloproteinases, and aggrecanases break down matrix faster than it is rebuilt, so cartilage loses water, softens, and cracks. Once cartilage thins, load falls directly on subchondral bone, which thickens, forms cysts, and grows marginal osteophytes. Because the driver is mechanical rather than systemic autoimmunity, stiffness is brief and the pattern follows the loaded joints.

points: Reduced bone mass with normal mineralization; trabecular bone is hit first.
Low peak bone mass plus age-related loss; estrogen loss raises RANKL and lowers osteoprotegerin, so osteoclasts resorb more.
Secondary causes: glucocorticoids, hyperthyroidism, immobilization, alcohol, smoking.
Fractures: vertebral compression (height loss, kyphosis), hip, distal radius.
Serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase normal.
DEXA T-score minus 2.5 or lower is osteoporosis; minus 1 to minus 2.5 is osteopenia.
notes.why: Bone mass in later life equals the peak reached in early adulthood minus what is lost afterward. Osteoblasts and stromal cells express RANKL, which binds RANK on osteoclast precursors to drive their formation, while osteoprotegerin is a decoy receptor that soaks up RANKL. Estrogen restrains RANKL and supports osteoprotegerin, so menopause tips the balance toward resorption. Trabecular bone has the largest remodeling surface, so it is lost first, which is why vertebrae and the distal radius fracture early, while normal mineralization keeps serum labs normal.

points: Overactive, huge osteoclasts start the disease, then osteoblasts lay down bone in a disorganized way.
Phases: lytic, mixed, then sclerotic (burned out); end result is thick but weak mosaic lamellar bone.
Older adults; skull, pelvis, spine, femur, tibia.
Isolated high alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium, phosphate, and PTH.
Complications: bone pain, enlarging skull (hat size), hearing loss, bowed tibia, fractures, high-output heart failure from arteriovenous shunting, osteosarcoma.
notes.why: The disease starts with huge, overactive osteoclasts, and osteoblasts answer by laying down new bone quickly and haphazardly, leaving irregular cement lines in a mosaic pattern. The new bone is thick and highly vascular but structurally weak, which explains bowing and fractures. Blood shunting through this hypervascular bone can raise cardiac output enough to cause high-output heart failure, and skull involvement can affect the ossicles or narrow foramina, causing hearing loss. Isolated high alkaline phosphatase reflects intense osteoblast work with normal mineral regulation.

points: Bone infarction when blood supply is cut off; femoral head is the most common site.
Causes: glucocorticoids, alcohol, sickle cell disease, SLE, decompression sickness, femoral neck and scaphoid fractures.
Femoral head depends on retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery.
MRI is the most sensitive test; early x-rays can be normal.
notes.why: Some bone regions have almost no collateral flow. The adult femoral head depends mainly on retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery running up the femoral neck, so a displaced neck fracture or vessel blockage infarcts it. Glucocorticoids and alcohol are thought to enlarge marrow fat cells and raise pressure inside bone, sickled cells block sinusoids, and nitrogen bubbles in decompression sickness occlude vessels. Dead trabeculae look normal on x-ray until collapse begins, while MRI shows marrow edema early.

points: Developmental dysplasia of the hip: newborn, often girl, breech; Ortolani test reduces a dislocated hip, Barlow test dislocates an unstable one.
Legg-Calve-Perthes: idiopathic femoral head osteonecrosis in young children (often boys about 4 to 8), painless or mildly painful limp.
Slipped capital femoral epiphysis: obese adolescent; the epiphysis slips off the femoral neck; hip or referred knee pain.
Osgood-Schlatter: traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle from patellar tendon pull in active teens.
Chondromalacia patellae: softened patellar cartilage, anterior knee pain worse with stairs or long sitting.
Osteochondritis dissecans: a fragment of subchondral bone and cartilage separates, causing pain, effusion, or locking.
notes.why: Each disorder reflects the weak point of the skeleton at that age. In the newborn, a shallow acetabulum and lax capsule let the femoral head slip out, and breech position adds abnormal force. In young children the femoral head epiphysis has a fragile blood supply, so interrupted flow causes Legg-Calve-Perthes disease. In adolescents the growth plate is the weakest zone, so obesity and shear displace the epiphysis (slipped capital femoral epiphysis), and repeated quadriceps pull through the patellar tendon irritates the tibial tubercle apophysis (Osgood-Schlatter disease).

points: Degenerated disc lets the nucleus pulposus herniate posterolaterally, where the posterior longitudinal ligament is thin.
Lumbar herniation compresses the lower root: L4 to L5 disc hits L5 (foot dorsiflexion, dorsum of foot).
Spondylosis is degenerative disc and facet change; spondylolisthesis is forward slip of one vertebra on the one below.
Dupuytren contracture: myofibroblast proliferation in the palmar fascia pulls the ring and little fingers into flexion.
notes.why: With age the nucleus pulposus loses proteoglycan and water and the annulus fibrosus develops fissures, so load can push nucleus material out. The posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow and reinforces only the midline, so herniation usually goes posterolateral. Each lumbar root leaves high in the foramen below its own vertebra, above the disc, so a posterolateral L4 to L5 herniation misses the exiting L4 root and compresses the traversing L5 root. In Dupuytren contracture, myofibroblasts contract and lay down collagen, shortening palmar fascia cords and pulling the fingers into flexion.

tricks.label: LOSS (osteoarthritis x-ray)
tricks.text: Loss of joint space, Osteophytes, Subchondral sclerosis, Subchondral cysts.

tricks.label: CASTS Bend LEGS (avascular necrosis)
tricks.text: Corticosteroids, Alcohol, Sickle cell, Trauma, SLE, the Bends (decompression), LEgg-Calve-Perthes, Gaucher disease, Slipped capital femoral epiphysis.

tricks.label: Heberden at the fingertip
tricks.text: Heberden nodes sit on the DIP joints, out at the fingertip. Bouchard nodes sit on the PIP joints, closer to the body. Both are osteophytes.

tricks.label: Lumbar disc names the lower root
tricks.text: In the lumbar spine the herniated disc usually hits the root that exits one level down: L4 to L5 disc, L5 root; L5 to S1 disc, S1 root.

highYield: Osteoarthritis is noninflammatory cartilage failure with eburnation, subchondral cysts, and osteophytes.
Osteoarthritis stiffness lasts under 30 minutes; rheumatoid arthritis stiffness lasts longer than an hour.
Osteoporosis has normal calcium, phosphate, and alkaline phosphatase; DEXA T-score of minus 2.5 or lower confirms it.
Estrogen loss raises RANKL-driven osteoclast resorption.
Paget disease: isolated high alkaline phosphatase, mosaic bone, high-output heart failure, osteosarcoma risk.
The femoral head is the most common site of avascular necrosis; MRI detects it first.
Obese adolescent with hip or knee pain suggests slipped capital femoral epiphysis.
L4 to L5 disc herniation compresses the L5 root.
pitfalls: Osteoporosis is less bone with normal mineral; osteomalacia is soft bone with poor mineral and abnormal labs.
Paget bone looks thick on x-ray but breaks easily.
Legg-Calve-Perthes affects younger children and is not linked to obesity; slipped capital femoral epiphysis affects obese teens.
Hip disease in children can show up as knee pain, so examine the hip in a limping child.
Spondylosis is wear and tear; spondylolysis is a pars defect; spondylolisthesis is the slip.

flows.title: Osteoarthritis
steps: Mechanical stress and aging injure chondrocytes.
Chondrocytes release MMPs and aggrecanases that degrade proteoglycan and type II collagen.
Cartilage loses water, softens, fibrillates, and cracks.
Exposed subchondral bone thickens and polishes (sclerosis and eburnation).
Synovial fluid forced into bone forms subchondral cysts.
Osteophytes grow at joint margins, limiting motion and causing pain.

flows.title: Postmenopausal osteoporosis
steps: Estrogen falls at menopause.
Osteoblasts and stromal cells raise RANKL and lower osteoprotegerin.
RANKL binds RANK, increasing osteoclast formation and activity.
Resorption exceeds formation, thinning trabecular bone first.
Vertebral bodies, hip, and distal radius fracture with minor trauma.

flows.title: Lumbar disc herniation at L4 to L5
steps: Nucleus pulposus dries out and the annulus fibrosus fissures with age.
Load pushes nucleus material out posterolaterally, beside the posterior longitudinal ligament.
The herniation compresses the traversing L5 root.
Radicular pain radiates down the leg (sciatica).
Weak foot dorsiflexion and great toe extension, numb dorsum of the foot.

summary: Musculoskeletal neoplasms include primary bone tumors, soft tissue sarcomas, and metastases. Exams test the patient's age, the location in the bone, the x-ray pattern, the tissue the tumor makes, and the gene or marker that confirms it.

points: Osteosarcoma: malignant cells make osteoid; most common primary malignant bone tumor apart from myeloma.
Peaks in adolescents and again in older adults with Paget disease or prior radiation.
Metaphysis around the knee (distal femur, proximal tibia).
X-ray: Codman triangle (lifted periosteum) and sunburst pattern.
Risk with germline RB1 (hereditary retinoblastoma) and TP53 (Li-Fraumeni) loss.
Spreads through blood, most often to the lungs.
Osteoid osteoma: under 2 cm cortical nidus with a sclerotic rim, young males, night pain relieved by NSAIDs because the nidus makes prostaglandin E2.
Osteoblastoma: larger, often in the vertebrae, pain not relieved by NSAIDs.
notes.why: Osteosarcoma is defined by malignant cells that make osteoid, and it arises where bone cells divide most: the knee metaphyses during the adolescent growth spurt, or pagetic or irradiated bone in older adults. RB and p53 normally halt the cell cycle and trigger apoptosis after DNA damage, so germline loss of either removes a key brake. The tumor lifts the periosteum, which lays down a triangle of reactive bone at its edge (Codman triangle). In osteoid osteoma the nidus makes prostaglandin E2 through cyclooxygenase, so NSAIDs block the source of pain.

points: Osteochondroma: most common benign bone tumor; metaphyseal bony stalk with a cartilage cap, continuous with the marrow; EXT1 or EXT2 (multiple in hereditary exostoses).
Enchondroma: hyaline cartilage inside the medullary cavity, often in hand bones; multiple in Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome (with hemangiomas).
Chondrosarcoma: malignant cartilage in older adults; pelvis, proximal femur, shoulder girdle.
Chondrosarcoma can arise from an enchondroma or osteochondroma and often carries IDH1 or IDH2 mutations.
notes.why: Osteochondroma forms when growth plate cartilage grows sideways out of the metaphysis, so the stalk's cortex and marrow are continuous with the host bone, and growth usually stops at skeletal maturity. EXT1 and EXT2 encode enzymes that build heparan sulfate, which shapes signaling gradients in the growth plate, so their loss lets chondrocytes escape normal orientation. Enchondromas are rests of growth plate cartilage left inside the medulla. Mutant IDH1 or IDH2 produces 2-hydroxyglutarate, an oncometabolite that alters DNA methylation and supports malignant change.

notes.h: Ewing sarcoma and giant cell tumors
points: Ewing sarcoma: children and adolescents; diaphysis of long bones or pelvis.
Small round blue cells, CD99 positive, EWSR1-FLI1 fusion from t(11;22).
Onion-skin periosteal reaction; fever, high ESR, and leukocytosis can mimic osteomyelitis.
Giant cell tumor of bone: young adults, epiphysis near the knee, soap-bubble lytic lesion.
Neoplastic stromal cells express RANKL and recruit osteoclast-like giant cells.
Tenosynovial giant cell tumor: tumor of synovium or tendon sheath driven by CSF1 overexpression.
notes.why: In Ewing sarcoma, the t(11;22) translocation fuses EWSR1 to FLI1 and creates an abnormal transcription factor that drives primitive cells to proliferate as small round blue cells. The tumor grows fast and lifts the periosteum in repeated layers (onion skin), and tumor necrosis and cytokines produce fever, high ESR, and leukocytosis that mimic infection. In giant cell tumor, the neoplastic cells are the mononuclear stromal cells; they express RANKL, which recruits benign osteoclast-like giant cells that do the bone destruction, so blocking RANKL with denosumab shrinks the tumor.

points: Rhabdomyosarcoma: most common soft tissue sarcoma of childhood; head and neck (orbit) or genitourinary tract.
Sarcoma botryoides: grape-like embryonal variant in the vagina or bladder of young children.
Rhabdomyoblasts stain for desmin and myogenin; alveolar type has PAX3 or PAX7 to FOXO1 fusions.
Leiomyosarcoma: adults; uterus and retroperitoneum; smooth muscle actin and desmin positive.
Sarcomas spread mainly through blood to the lungs; rhabdomyosarcoma can also reach lymph nodes.
notes.why: Rhabdomyosarcoma cells are arrested skeletal muscle precursors, so they express desmin, a muscle intermediate filament, and myogenin, a transcription factor of muscle differentiation. In the alveolar type, the PAX3 or PAX7 to FOXO1 fusion makes a strong transcriptional activator that blocks terminal differentiation, and this type has a worse prognosis than the embryonal type. Sarcomas arise in mesenchyme and invade thin-walled vessels early, so they spread mainly through blood, and the lungs, as the first capillary bed downstream, are the usual site of metastasis.

points: Metastases are the most common malignant bone tumors; they seed red marrow in the spine, pelvis, ribs, and proximal long bones.
Osteoblastic: prostate. Osteolytic: kidney, thyroid, lung. Mixed: breast.
Complications: pathologic fracture, hypercalcemia, pain, spinal cord compression.
Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy: clubbing, periosteal new bone on long bones, and arthritis as a paraneoplastic sign of lung cancer.
notes.why: Tumor cells reach bone through blood and settle in red marrow, where sinusoids are slow and fenestrated; the valveless vertebral venous plexus (Batson plexus) helps prostate and breast cancer reach the spine. In lytic metastases, tumor cells secrete PTHrP and cytokines that raise RANKL on osteoblasts, osteoclasts resorb bone, and growth factors released from matrix, such as TGF-beta, feed further tumor growth (the vicious cycle). Prostate cancer instead releases osteoblast stimulants such as endothelin-1, producing sclerotic lesions. Hypercalcemia comes from local osteolysis and from tumor PTHrP acting systemically.

tricks.label: Where in the bone
tricks.text: Epiphysis: giant cell tumor. Metaphysis: osteosarcoma and osteochondroma. Diaphysis: Ewing sarcoma. Location alone narrows most bone tumor questions.

tricks.label: Aspirin at night
tricks.text: A young man woken by bone pain that aspirin or ibuprofen relieves has osteoid osteoma; the nidus makes prostaglandin E2, which NSAIDs block.

highYield: Metastases are the most common malignant tumors in bone; prostate makes blastic lesions.
Osteosarcoma: teen with a metaphyseal knee tumor, Codman triangle, sunburst, lung metastasis.
Hereditary retinoblastoma (RB1) and Li-Fraumeni (TP53) raise osteosarcoma risk; Paget disease does in older adults.
Ewing sarcoma: diaphysis, onion skin, CD99, t(11;22) EWSR1-FLI1, may mimic osteomyelitis.
Chondrosarcoma: older adult, pelvis or shoulder, IDH1 or IDH2.
Rhabdomyosarcoma: most common childhood soft tissue sarcoma; desmin and myogenin.
Giant cell tumor of bone: epiphyseal soap bubble; stromal cells make RANKL.
Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy is a paraneoplastic sign of lung cancer.
pitfalls: Fever and high ESR with a child's bone lesion can be Ewing sarcoma, not just osteomyelitis.
Osteoid osteoma pain responds to NSAIDs; osteoblastoma pain does not.
Codman triangle shows aggressive growth but is not specific for osteosarcoma.
Multiple myeloma is the most common primary malignancy in bone, but it arises from plasma cells; that is why osteosarcoma is called the most common primary bone tumor apart from myeloma.
Myogenin marks skeletal muscle (rhabdomyosarcoma); smooth muscle actin marks smooth muscle (leiomyosarcoma).

flows.title: Osteolytic bone metastasis (vicious cycle)
steps: Tumor cells reach red marrow through blood, often via the vertebral venous plexus.
Tumor cells secrete PTHrP and cytokines in the bone microenvironment.
Osteoblasts and stromal cells raise RANKL expression.
Osteoclasts resorb bone, releasing calcium and stored TGF-beta.
TGF-beta stimulates tumor growth and more PTHrP, sustaining the cycle.
Lytic lesions cause pain, pathologic fracture, and hypercalcemia.

flows.title: Giant cell tumor of bone
steps: Neoplastic mononuclear stromal cells proliferate in the epiphysis.
Stromal cells express RANKL.
RANKL recruits and activates osteoclast-like giant cells.
Giant cells resorb bone, creating a soap-bubble lytic lesion.

flows.title: Hereditary retinoblastoma to osteosarcoma
steps: Germline RB1 mutation inactivates one allele in every cell.
A second somatic hit in a retinal cell causes childhood retinoblastoma.
A second hit in a dividing osteoblastic cell removes the G1 checkpoint.
Unchecked proliferation produces osteosarcoma, often in adolescence or a radiation field.

summary: Infectious musculoskeletal diseases include septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, necrotizing fasciitis, gangrene, and infective myositis. Exams test the likely organism for each patient, how the infection reaches the tissue, and the findings in joint fluid, bone, and skin.

points: Bacteria reach the joint through blood (most cases) or by direct inoculation (injection, surgery, bite).
The synovium is richly vascular with no basement membrane, so bacteria seed it easily.
Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause; Neisseria gonorrhoeae in sexually active young adults.
Risk: rheumatoid arthritis, prosthetic joints, injection drug use, diabetes, older age.
Neutrophil enzymes destroy cartilage within days, so a hot swollen joint is an emergency.
Gonococcal arthritis can be migratory with tenosynovitis and pustular skin lesions; joint cultures are often negative.
notes.why: Synovial capillaries are fenestrated and the synovial lining has no basement membrane, so bacteria in the blood cross easily into the joint, where synovial fluid supports their growth. Neutrophils pour in and release proteases and cytokines such as IL-1, which together with bacterial toxins break down cartilage matrix. Chondrocytes cannot replace lost cartilage, so damage done within days is permanent, which is why prompt drainage matters. Gonococcal infection has a bacteremic phase with tenosynovitis and skin lesions, and the organism is hard to culture from joint fluid.

points: Noninflammatory (osteoarthritis, trauma): clear, under 2,000 WBC/mm3, few neutrophils.
Inflammatory (rheumatoid arthritis, gout, pseudogout, reactive arthritis): cloudy, about 2,000 to 50,000 WBC/mm3, mostly neutrophils.
Septic: purulent, usually over 50,000 WBC/mm3, over 75 percent neutrophils, positive Gram stain or culture.
Gout: needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals. Pseudogout: rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals.
Crystals do not rule out infection; both can be present together.
notes.why: Synovial fluid is a plasma ultrafiltrate plus hyaluronic acid secreted by synovial cells, which makes normal fluid viscous and nearly acellular. Inflammation recruits neutrophils whose enzymes break down hyaluronic acid, so fluid becomes cloudy and thin as the white cell count rises along a continuum from inflammatory to septic. Under polarized light, monosodium urate is yellow when parallel to the compensator axis (negative birefringence), while calcium pyrophosphate is blue when parallel (positive). An inflamed joint with crystals can still be infected, so Gram stain and culture are still sent.

points: Children: blood-borne seeding of the long bone metaphysis, where slow flow in looping vessels and few phagocytes let bacteria settle.
Adults: vertebral osteomyelitis with discitis from blood spread, and contiguous spread from diabetic foot ulcers.
S. aureus is most common; Salmonella in sickle cell disease; Pseudomonas after a nail through a sneaker or in injection drug use; Mycobacterium tuberculosis in the spine (Pott disease).
Sequestrum is dead bone; involucrum is new bone around it; Brodie abscess is a walled-off bone abscess.
ESR and CRP are high; MRI is the most sensitive imaging; x-ray changes lag about 2 weeks.
Chronic osteomyelitis can drain through a sinus tract, which may develop squamous cell carcinoma.
notes.why: In a child's metaphysis, nutrient artery branches loop into wide venous sinusoids just below the growth plate, where flow slows and the vessel lining is discontinuous, so bacteria in the blood lodge there. Pus raises pressure in rigid bone, compresses vessels, and lifts the periosteum, cutting both inner and outer blood supply so a segment dies (sequestrum), while the lifted periosteum makes new bone around it (involucrum). Dead bone has no blood flow, so neutrophils and antibiotics cannot reach it and infection persists. In sickle cell disease, bowel infarcts and functional asplenia favor Salmonella.

points: Infection spreads rapidly along fascial planes and clots the vessels that feed the overlying skin.
Type I: polymicrobial (anaerobes plus aerobes), in diabetes or after surgery; Fournier gangrene of the perineum.
Type II: Streptococcus pyogenes (group A), alone or with S. aureus, can strike healthy people after minor injury.
Pain out of proportion to exam, swelling past the redness, crepitus, bullae, dusky skin, and systemic toxicity.
notes.why: Bacteria spread along the relatively avascular superficial fascia, and their toxins and enzymes (for group A streptococci, streptolysins, superantigen exotoxins, and hyaluronidase) dissolve tissue planes. Thrombosis of the perforating vessels that pass through the fascia to the skin starves the overlying tissue, which is why skin changes lag behind the deep infection and pain is out of proportion to what is seen. Gas-forming organisms in type I infection produce crepitus, and streptococcal superantigens can cause toxic shock.

points: Dry gangrene: arterial occlusion causes coagulative necrosis; black, shriveled, sharply demarcated.
Wet gangrene: bacteria infect the dead tissue, giving liquefactive necrosis; swollen, foul, spreading, risk of sepsis.
Diabetes and peripheral artery disease raise risk through poor perfusion, neuropathy, and weak neutrophil function.
Gas gangrene: Clostridium perfringens infects deep contaminated wounds; alpha toxin (lecithinase) destroys cell membranes.
Gas gangrene signs: rapid spread, severe pain, crepitus, bronze skin, hemolysis, and shock.
notes.why: The type of necrosis depends on whether protein denaturation or enzymatic digestion dominates. In dry gangrene, ischemia denatures proteins, including the cell's own enzymes, so the tissue keeps its outline as it dries and mummifies (coagulative necrosis). In wet gangrene, bacteria and recruited neutrophils release hydrolytic enzymes that digest tissue (liquefactive necrosis), and infection spreads into living tissue. Clostridium perfringens grows in anaerobic, devitalized tissue, ferments to make gas, and its alpha toxin is a phospholipase C (lecithinase) that splits membrane lecithin, lysing muscle cells and red blood cells.

points: Pyomyositis: S. aureus abscess in a large muscle such as the thigh or buttock.
Trichinellosis: Trichinella spiralis larvae from undercooked pork or wild game encyst in skeletal muscle.
Trichinellosis findings: myalgia, fever, periorbital edema, and eosinophilia.
notes.why: Skeletal muscle normally resists bacterial infection, so pyomyositis usually needs a predisposing factor such as trauma or immunosuppression plus S. aureus bacteremia. In trichinellosis, swallowed cysts release larvae in the small intestine, where they mature into adults that release new larvae; these travel through blood and lymph to striated muscle, where each larva turns a muscle cell into a nurse cell and encysts. The tissue-migrating parasite drives a Th2 response with IL-5, which explains the eosinophilia, and larval migration produces fever, myalgia, and periorbital edema.

tricks.label: Dead bone, new bone
tricks.text: Sequestrum is sequestered (dead and isolated). Involucrum is the envelope of new bone that wraps around it.

tricks.label: Dry is clean, wet is infected
tricks.text: Dry gangrene stays coagulative and sharply edged. Add bacteria and enzymes and it turns wet, liquefied, and spreading.

tricks.label: Pain out of proportion
tricks.text: Severe pain with skin that looks only mildly red points to a deep process: necrotizing fasciitis, gas gangrene, or compartment syndrome.

highYield: S. aureus is the top cause of septic arthritis and osteomyelitis.
Septic joint fluid usually has more than 50,000 WBC/mm3 with mostly neutrophils.
Childhood hematogenous osteomyelitis settles in the metaphysis because blood flow there is slow.
Salmonella osteomyelitis is classic in sickle cell disease; Pseudomonas follows a nail through a sneaker.
MRI is the most sensitive imaging for osteomyelitis.
Necrotizing fasciitis: pain out of proportion, crepitus, bullae; type II is group A streptococcus.
Clostridium perfringens alpha toxin (lecithinase) causes gas gangrene with hemolysis and shock.
Trichinella from undercooked pork or game causes myalgia, periorbital edema, and eosinophilia.
pitfalls: Finding crystals in a joint does not exclude infection; a gouty joint can also be septic.
Crepitus can occur in type I necrotizing fasciitis and in gas gangrene; Gram stain and the deep tissue involved (fascia versus muscle) help separate them.
Early osteomyelitis can have a normal x-ray; order MRI if suspicion is high.
Gonococcal arthritis often has negative joint cultures; test the urethra, cervix, rectum, and throat.

flows.title: Acute hematogenous osteomyelitis in a child
steps: Bacteremia, most often S. aureus, reaches the long bone metaphysis.
Slow flow in looping metaphyseal vessels lets bacteria lodge and multiply.
Neutrophil influx raises pressure in rigid bone and compresses vessels.
Pus lifts the periosteum, cutting off cortical blood supply.
The devascularized cortex dies, forming a sequestrum.
Lifted periosteum lays down new bone around it (involucrum).

flows.title: Necrotizing fasciitis
steps: Bacteria enter through a minor wound, surgical site, or ulcer.
Toxins and enzymes spread infection along the superficial fascia.
Perforating vessels to the skin thrombose.
Overlying skin becomes ischemic: dusky color, bullae, then necrosis.
Toxins and bacteremia cause shock and multiorgan failure.

flows.title: Septic arthritis
steps: Bacteremia seeds the vascular synovium, which lacks a basement membrane.
Bacteria multiply in synovial fluid, and neutrophils pour into the joint.
Neutrophil proteases, cytokines, and bacterial toxins degrade cartilage matrix.
Cartilage is lost within days and cannot regenerate.
Untreated, the joint is left with permanent arthritis.

summary: Musculoskeletal trauma covers fractures and how they heal, soft tissue injuries, and the dangerous complications of injury: avascular necrosis, nerve and artery damage, fat embolism, compartment syndrome, rhabdomyolysis, and myositis ossificans. Exams link each injury to the structure at risk and the mechanism of harm.

points: Hematoma and inflammation (first days): clot forms a fibrin scaffold; platelets and macrophages release growth factors.
Soft callus (about 1 to 3 weeks): granulation tissue and fibrocartilage bridge the gap.
Hard callus (weeks to months): woven bone replaces the cartilage by endochondral ossification.
Remodeling (months to years): woven bone becomes lamellar bone shaped along lines of stress.
Delayed union or nonunion: poor blood supply, infection, motion at the fracture, smoking, diabetes, malnutrition.
notes.why: Fracture healing repeats bone development. The hematoma provides a fibrin scaffold and growth factors such as PDGF, TGF-beta, and BMPs that recruit and activate progenitor cells from the periosteum and marrow. Where the gap is low in oxygen and moves slightly, progenitors become chondrocytes and form a soft callus, which is replaced by woven bone through endochondral ossification as vessels grow in. Coupled osteoclast and osteoblast remodeling then shapes lamellar bone to the loads it bears (Wolff law), so poor blood supply or excess motion stalls the process.

points: Scaphoid: blood enters distally and flows backward, so the proximal pole can die (avascular necrosis, nonunion).
Femoral neck: displaced fractures tear the retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery, causing femoral head necrosis.
Supracondylar humerus (child): brachial artery and median nerve injury; can lead to forearm compartment syndrome.
Long bone and pelvic fractures: fat embolism about 1 to 3 days later.
Fat embolism triad: hypoxemia, confusion, and petechiae (chest, axillae, conjunctivae).
notes.why: Blood supply anatomy decides which fragment dies. The scaphoid's main supply from the radial artery enters the distal pole and runs proximally, so a waist fracture cuts off the proximal pole. In an extension-type supracondylar fracture in a child, the sharp proximal fragment is driven forward into the brachial artery and median nerve, which lie directly in front of the distal humerus. In fat embolism, marrow fat enters torn veins, lodges in lung and systemic capillaries, and is broken down into free fatty acids that injure endothelium, which explains the 1 to 3 day delay.

points: Sprain: ligament stretch or tear. Strain: muscle or tendon stretch or tear.
Contusion: bleeding into soft tissue from a blow. Dislocation: joint surfaces lose contact.
Ligaments heal slowly: dense regular tissue with poor blood supply and few fibroblasts; repair forms weaker scar.
notes.why: Ligaments and tendons are dense regular connective tissue with parallel type I collagen bundles, few fibroblasts, and little blood flow, so repair after a tear is slow and forms less organized scar. The early repair collagen is rich in type III and remodels gradually, but the healed ligament rarely regains full tensile strength, which explains recurrent sprains and joint instability. Muscle heals better because satellite cells can regenerate fibers when the basal lamina is intact, though large tears still heal with scar.

points: Swelling in a closed fascial compartment raises pressure until capillary and venous flow stop.
Causes: tibial and forearm fractures, crush injury, reperfusion after ischemia, tight casts, circumferential burns.
Earliest signs: pain out of proportion and pain with passive stretch of the compartment's muscles.
Pulses are usually preserved early because arterial pressure is higher than compartment pressure.
Untreated forearm compartment syndrome leaves Volkmann ischemic contracture (fibrosed forearm flexors, flexed wrist, and clawed fingers).
notes.why: Fascia does not stretch, so swelling in a compartment raises tissue pressure, and once it exceeds capillary and venous pressure, flow to muscle and nerve stops even though arterial pressure still keeps pulses present. Ischemia makes capillaries leak more fluid, which raises pressure further in a self-sustaining cycle. Ischemic muscle is intensely painful, and stretching it passively worsens the pain, which is the earliest reliable sign. Muscle dies within hours and is replaced by fibrous tissue that shortens, giving Volkmann contracture in the forearm.

points: Muscle breakdown from crush injury, extreme exertion, heat, seizures, statins, or drugs and alcohol.
Dying muscle releases CK, myoglobin, potassium, and phosphate.
CK very high (often over 5 times normal, frequently many thousands of U/L).
Urine dipstick positive for blood with few or no red cells on microscopy (myoglobinuria); tea-colored urine.
Hyperkalemia can cause arrhythmia; calcium is often low early as it deposits in injured muscle.
Acute kidney injury from myoglobin casts, heme toxicity to tubules, and renal vasoconstriction.
notes.why: When muscle cells are crushed or run out of ATP, the sodium-potassium and calcium pumps fail, intracellular calcium rises, and proteases destroy the cell, spilling its contents. Myoglobin is small enough to be filtered, and in acidic tubular fluid it forms casts with Tamm-Horsfall protein, while its heme iron causes oxidative tubular injury and scavenges nitric oxide, causing vasoconstriction. The dipstick reacts to the peroxidase activity of heme in myoglobin, so it reads positive for blood without red cells. Released potassium and phosphate rise, and calcium deposits in damaged muscle.

points: Heterotopic bone forms in muscle after trauma, often in the thigh or upper arm of young athletes.
Zonal pattern: mature bone at the periphery, immature cells in the center.
Osteosarcoma shows the opposite: the most mature, mineralized tissue centrally with an infiltrative, atypical edge.
notes.why: After muscle trauma, mesenchymal progenitor cells in the injured tissue differentiate into osteoblasts and form bone that matures from the outside in. The zonal pattern, a peripheral shell of mature bone around a cellular, immature center, is the reverse of osteosarcoma, in which the most atypical, proliferating cells sit at the infiltrative edge. Recognizing this pattern keeps a benign reactive lesion from being mistaken for a malignant tumor, especially in a young athlete with a recent injury.

tricks.label: Sprain versus strain
tricks.text: Strain has a T for tendon (and the muscle it belongs to). Sprain is the ligament.

tricks.label: The 6 Ps
tricks.text: Pain, Pallor, Paresthesia, Paralysis, Pulselessness, Poikilothermia. In compartment syndrome pain comes first; pulselessness comes late.

tricks.label: Blood but no red cells
tricks.text: A dipstick positive for blood with no red cells on microscopy means heme pigment: myoglobin (rhabdomyolysis) or free hemoglobin (hemolysis).

highYield: Fracture healing order: hematoma, soft callus, hard callus, remodeling.
Scaphoid fractures risk proximal pole avascular necrosis because blood flows in from the distal end.
Displaced femoral neck fractures risk femoral head necrosis.
Supracondylar humerus fractures injure the brachial artery and median nerve.
Fat embolism after long bone fracture: hypoxemia, confusion, petechiae.
Compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch, with pulses often still present.
Rhabdomyolysis: very high CK, heme-positive urine without red cells, hyperkalemia, acute kidney injury.
Myositis ossificans matures from the outside in; osteosarcoma does the reverse.
pitfalls: A palpable pulse does not rule out compartment syndrome.
A normal first x-ray does not rule out a scaphoid fracture when the anatomic snuffbox is tender.
Fat embolism is delayed by a day or more, which helps separate it from immediate hemorrhage or pneumothorax.
Myositis ossificans can look worrying on biopsy; the orderly zonal pattern points away from osteosarcoma.

dumps.p: Draw a fractured long bone at four stages of healing. Label the cells and tissue present at each stage.
l: Stage 1: hematoma with fibrin, platelets, and inflammatory cells
Growth factors from platelets and macrophages recruit repair cells
Stage 2: soft callus of granulation tissue and fibrocartilage
Stage 3: hard callus of woven bone by endochondral ossification
Stage 4: remodeling to lamellar bone by osteoclasts and osteoblasts
Lists two causes of delayed union (for example poor blood supply, smoking, infection, motion)

dumps.p: Trace what happens after a leg is crushed under a heavy object for several hours. Draw arrows from the muscle to the heart and kidney.
l: Swollen muscle raises compartment pressure
Capillary and venous flow stop, causing muscle and nerve ischemia
Muscle cells break down and release CK, myoglobin, potassium, and phosphate
Hyperkalemia threatens cardiac arrhythmia
Myoglobin forms tubular casts and injures tubules
Acute kidney injury follows
Urine is heme positive with few red cells

flows.title: Fracture healing
steps: Torn vessels form a hematoma that clots into a fibrin scaffold.
Platelets and macrophages release PDGF, TGF-beta, and BMPs.
Progenitor cells form granulation tissue and fibrocartilage: soft callus.
Endochondral ossification replaces cartilage with woven bone: hard callus.
Osteoclasts and osteoblasts remodel woven bone into lamellar bone along stress lines.

flows.title: Rhabdomyolysis to acute kidney injury
steps: Crush, exertion, or toxins deplete muscle ATP and injure the sarcolemma.
Intracellular calcium rises, activating proteases that destroy muscle cells.
Myoglobin, potassium, phosphate, and CK enter the blood.
Filtered myoglobin forms tubular casts, and heme injures tubular cells.
Renal vasoconstriction and tubular obstruction cause acute kidney injury.

flows.title: Compartment syndrome
steps: Fracture, crush, or reperfusion causes swelling inside an inelastic fascial compartment.
Compartment pressure rises above capillary and venous pressure.
Muscle and nerve perfusion stop while arterial pulses persist.
Ischemia increases capillary leak, raising pressure further.
Untreated, muscle necroses and is replaced by contracting fibrous tissue.
